title: Version3 primary-source market refresh
summary: Nine retrieved source entries and ten inspected job descriptions across three employers and five listed countries. A targeted qualitative sample, not a representative global vacancy survey.

methodology.reports: Read official report/occupation pages and distinguish projections, employer expectations, research synthesis, and engineering guidance.
methodology.sampling: Purposively selected distinct roles from public Anthropic, Elastic, and Datadog Greenhouse feeds to span product, research, infrastructure, domain integration, and internship work. Geography variants of the same principal role were not separately counted.
methodology.retrieval: HTTPS through the inherited session proxy; TLS verification retained. Initial sandbox socket denial resolved by authorized read-only execution escalation.
limitations: Three technology employers are not representative of all global companies or industries.
Sample overrepresents established AI/enterprise companies and experienced roles.
No job requirement prevalence, global vacancy estimate, salary forecast, personal employment probability, or causal effect was estimated.
Board presence establishes listed content at retrieval, not that a vacancy is still accepting applications later.
Eligibility is not inferred from a location label; internships have concrete student, calendar, and location constraints.
Sources contain different observation periods; publication/update dates are kept separate from retrieval dates.

sources.title: Occupational Outlook Handbook: Data Scientists
sources.scope: United States; data scientists; 2025–2035 projection period
sources.verification: Retrieved successfully over HTTPS; quoted passage matched captured text. Underlying study results were not independently reproduced.
findings: BLS projects 35% employment growth for data scientists over 2025–2035 and about 24,800 openings per year on average, including replacement needs.
The page lists a bachelor’s degree as typical entry-level education and describes coding, statistical reasoning, visualization, and communication as part of the occupation.
limitations: This is a US occupational projection, not an observed count of current vacancies.
Annual openings include replacements; they are not all new jobs, remote jobs, or junior positions.
Typical educational attainment does not establish the requirements of every employer.
sources.excerpt: Employment of data scientists is projected to grow 35 percent from 2025 to 2035, much faster than the average for all occupations.
implications: Retain statistics, coding, analysis, and explanation in the common core.
Do not turn occupational growth into a personal employment probability.

sources.title: Occupational Outlook Handbook: Software Developers, Quality Assurance Analysts, and Testers
sources.scope: United States; combined software developer/QA/tester occupation group;2025–2035
sources.verification: Retrieved successfully over HTTPS; quoted passage matched captured text. Underlying study results were not independently reproduced.
findings: BLS projects 10% growth for the combined occupation group over 2025–2035 and about 106,100 average annual openings.
The described work includes understanding user needs, building software, testing it, and communicating with technical and nontechnical collaborators.
limitations: The 10% figure applies to the combined group, not specifically ML engineering or software developers alone.
US projections do not establish global opportunities or the accessibility of entry-level roles.
sources.excerpt: Overall employment of software developers, quality assurance analysts, and testers is projected to grow 10 percent from 2025 to 2035, much faster than the average for all occupations.
implications: Make software fundamentals, tests, deployment, and communication first-class learning outcomes.

sources.title: The Future of Jobs Report 2025
sources.scope: Over 1,000 employers, more than 14 million represented workers,22 industry clusters,55 economies; expectations for 2025–2030
sources.verification: Retrieved successfully over HTTPS; quoted passage matched captured text. Underlying study results were not independently reproduced.
findings: The surveyed employers rank analytical thinking as a central current skill and AI/big data, networks/cybersecurity, and technological literacy among the fastest-growing skill areas.
The report estimates 39% of existing skill sets could change or become outdated over 2025–2030; this is a survey-based expectation, not a realized outcome.
limitations: Employer expectations are forecasts, not causal evidence or guaranteed outcomes.
The employer sample is not the entire global labor market and is not a junior AI-job vacancy census.
The report predates this 2026 research refresh; its forecasts have not been treated as current observed facts.
sources.excerpt: AI and big data top the list of fastest-growing skills, followed closely by networks and cybersecurity as well as technology literacy.
implications: Combine technical depth with analytical reasoning, security awareness, and adaptation.
Keep frameworks replaceable while preserving mathematical and engineering foundations.

sources.title: AI Index 2026: Economy
sources.publisher: Stanford Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence
sources.published: 2026 (report edition; exact publication day not established here)
sources.scope: Multiple economic datasets and studies summarized in the 2026 report; geographical scope varies by claim
sources.verification: Retrieved successfully over HTTPS; quoted passage matched captured text. Underlying study results were not independently reproduced.
findings: The chapter distinguishes rising organizational adoption from uneven labor-market effects and describes particular pressure in hiring pipelines and younger exposed workers.
It separates organizations’ expectations of workforce reductions from observed aggregate employment and describes productivity benefits as task-dependent.
limitations: The chapter is a synthesis of studies with different populations and methods; their results must not be combined into a single causal estimate.
This refresh read the official chapter summary rather than independently reproducing all underlying studies.
Neither organizational adoption nor frontier-model benchmark performance is a measure of junior job availability.
sources.excerpt: AI's labor market effects are showing up unevenly, concentrated in hiring pipelines and the youngest workers in exposed occupations.
implications: Require demonstrable independent debugging and transfer, alongside measured AI-assisted work.
Treat entry-level access as a separate problem from broad AI adoption.

sources.title: Rules of Machine Learning: Best Practices for ML Engineering
sources.scope: Engineering advice based on production ML practice; not labor-market measurement
sources.verification: Retrieved successfully over HTTPS; quoted passage matched captured text. Underlying study results were not independently reproduced.
findings: The guide recommends metrics before model sophistication, simple initial models, and infrastructure tested separately from learning components.
It treats interpretable baselines and trustworthy pipelines as practical debugging tools.
limitations: This is engineering guidance, not a survey of hiring requirements or a guarantee that one model class fits every task.
sources.excerpt: Rule #4: Keep the first model simple and get the infrastructure right.
implications: Every ML capstone should start with a measurable simple baseline and an inspectable data path.

sources.title: Common pitfalls and recommended practices
sources.scope: Model evaluation, preprocessing, leakage, and reproducibility in scikit-learn
sources.verification: Retrieved successfully over HTTPS; quoted passage matched captured text. Underlying study results were not independently reproduced.
findings: The documentation explains that leakage uses information unavailable at prediction time and creates overly optimistic performance estimates.
It recommends splitting before learned preprocessing, keeping test data out of fit/fit_transform, and using pipelines to reduce mistakes.
limitations: The stable documentation can change; retrieval date and captured hash identify this reading.
A pipeline does not automatically prevent every leakage mechanism; time/group splitting and label availability still require problem-specific reasoning.
sources.excerpt: Data leakage occurs when information that would not be available at prediction time is used when building the model.
implications: Make leakage checks a critical assessment gate that cannot be averaged away by other good scores.

implications.title: Build the software core first
implications.decision: Retain Python, data structures, debugging, tests, Git, HTTP/API behavior, and clear writing before specialization.
implications.artifact: A small application another person can run, test, and understand.

implications.title: Make evaluation a recurring gate
implications.decision: Require baselines, a leakage-safe split, failure analysis, and task-specific evaluation in ML/LLM projects.
implications.artifact: A versioned test/evaluation set and a report explaining why the result is trustworthy.

implications.title: Teach production behavior rather than tool lists
implications.decision: Use data contracts, authentication, validation, retries, observability, and budget limits as project requirements; frameworks are interchangeable implementations.
implications.artifact: An instrumented service with known failure modes, recovery behavior, and a cost/latency envelope.

implications.title: Keep research and systems specialization explicit
implications.decision: Offer deeper mathematics, paper reproduction, distributed training, profiling, and GPU topics after the common trunk; state the additional educational/experience requirements seen in relevant roles.
implications.artifact: A reproducible experiment with ablations, or a benchmark with correctness and resource constraints.

implications.title: Separate entry access from long-term demand
implications.decision: Do not equate occupational growth with easy junior entry. Track region, graduation, degree, experience, and work-authorization constraints before recommending an application.
implications.artifact: A personal eligibility-aware opportunity ledger and portfolio-to-requirement mapping.

implications.title: Preserve independent thinking alongside AI assistance
implications.decision: Record assistance honestly, require unaided transfer/debugging checks, and measure quality/time on real tasks instead of assuming universal productivity gains.
implications.artifact: An explanation and fresh debugging task completed under stated assistance conditions.

futureScenarios.condition: If models and coding assistance keep improving
futureScenarios.response: Invest in problem definition, data quality, evaluation, integration, and independent debugging.
futureScenarios.status: Curriculum judgment, not a labor-demand forecast.

futureScenarios.condition: If inference cost, latency, or reliability becomes a binding product constraint
futureScenarios.response: Prioritize measurement, serving efficiency, caching, instrumentation, and failure handling.
futureScenarios.status: Conditional engineering response, not a prediction of job counts.

futureScenarios.condition: If a preferred framework loses relevance
futureScenarios.response: Retain portable foundations and a project whose behavior can be reproduced with a different implementation.
futureScenarios.status: Risk-management judgment, not a claim about which framework will win.
